prime.problem: If you think "faster chip = faster tokens", you'll buy compute that sits idle. Token generation is limited by how fast memory can feed the weights to the chip, and one division predicts it.
prime.fits: First mechanism card. The metric cards measured output speed; this card explains what sets it. Hardware, quantization, MoE and speculative decoding each attack one side of the division introduced here.
prime.goal: Estimate a model's token-speed ceiling on a given chip, and say which lever raises it.

attend: Why does writing each new token require reading every active weight again?
Why is the chip's math capacity nearly irrelevant for one user writing a long answer?
Why does prefill run at about 207 t/s on the M3 when decode runs at 15.4?
4× the bandwidth gave 3.1× the speed across Apple chips. What explains the gap?
Under which three conditions does bandwidth stop being the bottleneck?

must: Each decode step produces one token and needs every active weight → the whole model streams from memory once per token → little math per byte → speed ≈ bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token
Two ways to go faster → shrink the bytes (quantization, MoE, smaller model) or raise the bandwidth (better hardware) → every speed lever maps onto one side of the division
Prefill processes many prompt tokens per weight read → each byte is reused many times → compute-bound, not memory-bound → prompt reading is over 13× faster per token than writing on the M3
elevated: Real runs reach only part of the ceiling (44% for qwen3.5 on the M3, 58–75% for Llama 7B) → software overhead and attention reads matter → use the ceiling as an upper bound, not a prediction

compress.prompt: From memory, write the ceiling formula and compute the M3's ceiling for qwen3.5:4b. Then draw the division with arrows pointing into the numerator and denominator from each lever you know.
checklist: ceiling ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token
qwen3.5:4b Q4_K_M ≈ 2.85 GB/token; 100 GB/s ÷ 2.85 ≈ 35 t/s; measured 15.4
quantization, MoE, smaller model → fewer bytes
prefill and big batches reuse each weight, so they aren't bandwidth-bound in the same way

retrieve.q: Explain why generation is memory-bound but reading the prompt is not, using how many tokens share one read of the weights.
answer: decode: one token per full weight read, so time ≈ bytes ÷ bandwidth
prefill: all prompt tokens processed per weight read, so each byte serves many tokens
prefill becomes limited by compute instead

retrieve.q: Compute the ceiling for Llama 7B Q4_0 (about 3.5 GB) on an M3 Pro (150 GB/s) and compare it with the measured 30.74 t/s.
answer: the rest is lost to overhead and non-weight memory traffic

retrieve.q: You can either buy a chip with 2× the TFLOPS or one with 2× the memory bandwidth, for single-user chat. Which helps and why? When would the other one win?
answer: bandwidth: decode waits on memory, so it scales with bandwidth
compute helps prefill-heavy work (huge prompts) and heavily batched serving
for one user writing long answers, bandwidth wins

compare.q: This card uses one division; the roofline adds arithmetic intensity. What does the roofline explain that the division can't, and at what batch size does this card's rule stop working?
answer: roofline: speed is limited by min(compute, bandwidth × intensity)
decode at batch 1 has very low intensity, so the bandwidth side binds
as batch grows, each weight read serves more tokens and eventually compute binds; the bandwidth rule then overestimates the slowdown

compare.q: Bandwidth sets the time per token; length sets the number of tokens. If you could change only one on your M3, which would you pick for a 653-token answer, and why?
answer: bandwidth needs new hardware: at most ~3–4× within Apple chips
length is free: 653 → 82 tokens cuts about 7.9×
pick length unless the answer genuinely needs to be long

predict.q: Predict the M3's ceiling for a hypothetical 8B dense model at Q8 (about 8.5 bits per weight) and whether it will feel faster or slower than your qwen3.5:4b at Q4. Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: 8B × 8.5 ÷ 8 ≈ 8.5 GB per token → 100 ÷ 8.5 ≈ 12 t/s ceiling, below the 4B Q4's 35 t/s ceiling and even below its measured 15.4. It will feel about 3× slower in ceiling terms: twice the parameters and nearly twice the bits each means about 3× the bytes.

apply.task: Compute the speed ceiling for three models on your own machine (look up its memory bandwidth): the one you use now, a model twice its size at the same quantization, and your current model at 8-bit. Then run the one you have and compute what % of the ceiling you reach.
apply.done: You have three ceilings from bandwidth ÷ bytes, one measured speed, and its % of ceiling. You can say which change would help most on your machine.
apply.hint: bytes per token ≈ parameters × bits per weight ÷ 8. For the M3: 100 GB/s.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how bits and parameter count combine into bytes per token?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why prefill escapes the bandwidth limit?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: bytes per token → ceiling, or ceiling → measured speed?
Did you previously believe more TFLOPS meant faster chat? What changed?
Which side of the division do you expect the hardware card to move, and by how much?
